power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Factors influencing well-being judgments
table.research_questions:
Our primary question is to try to understand whether there are factors that differentially influence how people make judgments about their current and future well-being. We are specifically focusing on factors related to their stable personality traits, like optimism, their past circumstances, like their childhood environment, and their current circumstances, like their current relationships. Past circumstances
Confirmatory:
We hypothesize that positive past circumstances will be positively associated with both current well-being and future well-being.
Exploratory:
We will explore whether past circumstances predict future well-being when controlling for current well-being.

Identity/personality	
Confirmatory:
We hypothesize that positive aspects of identity and personality will be positively associated with both current well-being and future well-being. 

Current circumstances
Confirmatory:
We hypothesize that positive current circumstances will be positively associated with current well-being. 
Exploratory:
We will explore whether current circumstances predict current well-being when controlling for future well-being

table.description: We will be examining how their past circumstances influence their current and future well-being.
table.scale_index_aggregation:
# Preclassification of Variables

Variables in this study have been pre-classified into three key theoretical categories:

- Past Circumstances: Variables that represent early life experiences or historical factors (e.g., FATHER_LOVED, ABUSED, HEALTH_GROWUP).
- Identity/Personality: Variables reflecting personal traits, psychological factors, and beliefs (e.g., TRAITS1, BELONGING, APPROVE_GOVT).
- Current Circumstances: Variables related to present-day life conditions, such as socioeconomic status and health (e.g., AGE, INCOME, PHYSICAL_HLTH, CIGARETTES).

This preclassification is implemented through pre-coded R scripts, grouping variables conceptually for later analysis in models such as group penalized regression (grpreg) and Sparse Group Lasso (SGL).

# Variable Grouping

The R code implements the variable classification and prepares the data for analysis. Here's a breakdown of the process:
Variable Grouping
var_past_circumstances <- c(var_past_circumstances_either, var_past_circumstances_positive, var_past_circumstances_negative)
var_identity_personality <- c(var_identity_personality_either, var_identity_personality_positive, var_identity_personality_negative)
var_current_circumstances <- c(var_current_circumstances_either, var_current_circumstances_positive, var_current_circumstances_negative)

This code combines pre-defined lists of variables into three main categories: past circumstances, identity/personality, and current circumstances. Each category includes variables classified as either positive, negative, or neutral ("either").

# Create classification dataframe
hypotheses <- data.frame(variable = names(df_sweden_clean)) %>%
  mutate(
    past_circumstances = ifelse(variable %in% var_past_circumstances, 1, 0),
    identity_personality = ifelse(variable %in% var_identity_personality, 1, 0),
    current_circumstances = ifelse(variable %in% var_current_circumstances, 1, 0),
    positive = ifelse(variable %in% var_positive, 1, 0),
    negative = ifelse(variable %in% var_negative, 1, 0)
  )
This code creates a data frame called hypotheses that includes all variables from the main dataset (df_sweden_clean). It then adds binary indicators (1 or 0) for each classification:

- Which theoretical category the variable belongs to (past circumstances, identity/personality, or current circumstances)
- Whether the variable is considered positive or negative


predictor_hypotheses$group <- case_when(
  predictor_hypotheses$past_circumstances == 1 ~ 1,
  predictor_hypotheses$identity_personality == 1 ~ 2,
  predictor_hypotheses$current_circumstances == 1 ~ 3
)

This code assigns a group number to each predictor variable. This grouping vector (predictor_hypotheses$group) is passed into the models to ensure that variables from the same theoretical construct are treated together.

# Cleaning

Each of the variables has a precoded r function that transforms the data. This script can be found in scripts/data_cleaning_functions.R

# Documentation and Tracking
Although the current scripts are based on the study codebook and synthetic data,  adjustments may be needed if discrepancies arise with real data. All changes to data cleaning functions are documented through GitHub. You can review the edit history of our data cleaning scripts here: GitHub Commit History https://github.com/R-Computing-Lab/currentfuturewellbeing/commits/main/scripts/data_cleaning_functions.R, which can be accessed via the osf project.
table.units_of_analysis: The unit of analysis is the approximately 200,000 individual survey respondents from Wave 1. All respondents in the project’s finalized analysis dataset across the 22 countries are eligible. We are not preregistering any country or subgroup exclusions. We are not preregistering any content-based exclusions. Outlier handling and missing-data handling are addressed in subsequent sections and do not remove units at this stage.
table.missing_data_handling: Analyses use complete cases for the variables that enter a given model. There is no imputation in the preregistered analyses. The sample size used in each model is reported.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: We will not exclude extreme observations based on univariate or multivariate outlier flags. Penalized models will be fit on the full analysis dataset for each outcome. The only exception to this will be if there are impossible values as determined by the codebook, such as someone reporting a negative age. All such impossible values will be documented in the reproducible R script as well as timestamped via the GitHub repo attached to this osf project
table.sampling_weights: Primary analyses are unweighted because regularization methods do not natively accommodate complex survey features in a standard way.
table.statistical_tests:
We will use three main statistical models: group penalized regression (grpreg), Stochastic Search Variable Selection (SSVS), and Sparse Group Lasso (SGL). These models offer different strengths in identifying relevant predictors, accounting for group structures where applicable, and controlling for overfitting in high-dimensional data. 

The scripts for these specific models have already been written, and can be found and a time stamped version of these scribes can be found here https://github.com/R-Computing-Lab/currentfuturewellbeing/commit/500ade5936431f653421d9d8ad5b5ca1d5a6060c (this should be accessible via the connected project)
table.inference_criteria:
Primary evidence is based on variable selection and sign from prespecified models rather than null hypothesis tests.

Specifically, for penalized models
a) Group lasso and sparse group lasso are tuned by cross validation. The primary model is the lambda that minimizes cross validated error. The sensitivity model uses the one standard error rule.
b) Selection rule: a predictor is considered selected if its coefficient is nonzero at the chosen lambda.
c) Direction: the sign of the coefficient in the selected model.
d) Model fit summaries: cross validated mean squared error and cross validated R2 are reported. There are no p values or Bayes factors for penalized selections.

Bayesian SSVS
a) Evidence metric: posterior inclusion probability for each predictor.
b) Selection rule: posterior inclusion probability greater than 0.50.
c) Direction and uncertainty: posterior mean and a 95 percent credible interval. We do not compute Bayes factors.

Convergence across methods
a) A predictor is called convergent if it is selected by the primary penalized method and at least one complementary method with the same sign.
b) A predictor is called robust if it is selected by all three methods with the same sign.
c) Conclusions emphasize convergent predictors. Method-specific selections that are not convergent are reported but not interpreted as robust findings.

Incremental prediction for future wellbeing
For WB_FIVEYRS, each method is run twice, without and with WB_TODAY as a covariate. The preregistered confirmatory claim is supported if at least one positive past circumstance predictor is convergent with a positive sign in the model that includes WB_TODAY.

Post-selection descriptive tests
To quantify effects for communication, we fit linear models on the union of predictors selected by the primary method for each outcome. These are descriptive only.
table.exploratory_unplanned_tests: We may generate hypothesis-forming summaries from the model objects already produced in the Rmd (grpreg_results, sparsegl_results, ssvs_results, and the hypotheses table). Specifically, after the preregistered analyses, we will descriptively compare which predictors were selected by different methods and which were selected for WB_TODAY versus WB_FIVEYRS, and we will summarize selection counts by the three preregistered domains using the existing group labels. These comparisons will be presented as tables or plots derived from the stored coefficients at lambda.min for the penalized models and posterior inclusion probabilities for SSVS

The R code implements the variable classification and prepares the data for analysis. Here's a breakdown of the process:
Variable Grouping
var_past_circumstances <- c(var_past_circumstances_either, var_past_circumstances_positive, var_past_circumstances_negative)

This code combines pre-defined lists of variables into three main categories: past circumstances, identity/personality, and current circumstances. Each category includes variables classified as either positive, negative, or neutral (\"either\").

)
This code creates a data frame called hypotheses that includes all variables from the main dataset (df_sweden_clean). It then adds binary indicators (1 or 0) for each classification:

- Whether the variable is considered positive or negative

This code assigns a group number to each predictor variable. This grouping vector (predictor_hypotheses$group) is passed into the models to ensure that variables from the same theoretical construct are treated together.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 8 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: The GFS is a longitudinal study that examines factors contributing to human flourishing in a large, internationally diverse sample spanning 22 countries and territories, with approximately 200,000 participants enrolled at Wave 1 (Johnson et al., 2024; VanderWeele et al., 2025).
Participants were asked, "On which step of the ladder would you say you personally feel you stand at this time?"
Participants were asked, "Just your best guess, on which step do you think you will stand in the future, say about five years from now?"

report: #### SPSS data without syntax

An SPSS data file (`.sav`/`.por`) is present but **no SPSS syntax file (`.sps`) was found**, so the analysis that produced the results cannot be reproduced from the deposit. This is treated as a reproducibility failure (red). Consider depositing the analysis in **jamovi** (`.omv`) or **JASP** (`.jasp`) instead: these formats store the data and the analyses together in one file, so the results are reproducible from the file itself.
#### Stata data without syntax

A Stata data file (`.dta`) is present but **no Stata syntax file (`.do`) or output log (`.smcl`) was found**, so the analysis that produced the results cannot be reproduced from the deposit. This is treated as a reproducibility failure (red). Consider depositing the `.do` file (or, at minimum, a `.smcl`/`.log` output file, which at least records the exact commands that were run).

info.title: Current and Expected Well-Being in a Global Sample: The Role of Past Experiences, Current Circumstances, and Identity and Personality

text.text: People may use different processes to judge their current versus expected well-being.

Using Wave 1 of the Global Flourishing Study (N = 98,412; 22 countries), we examined how predictors spanning past experiences, current circumstances, and identity and personality were associated with current and expected (five-year) well-being.
We used stochastic search variable selection, a Bayesian method, to identify predictors reliably associated with each outcome, and focused interpretation on those with at least small effects.
Participants generally expected their future well-being to exceed their current well-being.

When each judgment was adjusted for the other, age and hope for the future showed opposite patterns: older participants reported lower, and more hopeful participants higher, expected well-being when controlling for current well-being.

Much of the explained variance was shared across domains, and past experiences contributed little unique variance once current circumstances and identity and personality were accounted for; this suggests that the past may matter for well-being judgments largely through its links to people's present lives.

Our findings demonstrate that current and expected well-being draw on largely overlapping information that is weighted differently depending on whether people evaluate their current or expected lives.
judgments center the future, which likely involves considering how one's circumstances may change and imagining how one will feel about them (Gilbert & Wilson, 2007).
text.formatted: judgments center the future, which likely involves considering how one's circumstances may change and imagining how one will feel about them <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Gilbert & Wilson, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Expected wellbeing may therefore draw on much of the same information as current well-being, weighted differently, with greater reliance on factors such as general optimism, beliefs about one's prospects, and the amount of time one expects to have ahead (Busseri et al., 2009; Carstensen, 2006; Lang et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Expected wellbeing may therefore draw on much of the same information as current well-being, weighted differently, with greater reliance on factors such as general optimism, beliefs about one's prospects, and the amount of time one expects to have ahead <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Busseri et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Carstensen, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lang et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals often expect their future well-being to surpass their current well-being.
People generally perceive their lives as improving from the past to the present and expect continued gains into the future (Röcke & Lachman, 2008).
text.formatted: People generally perceive their lives as improving from the past to the present and expect continued gains into the future <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Röcke & Lachman, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, individuals anticipate experiencing more positive than negative future events (Newby-Clark & Ross, 2003).
text.formatted: Similarly, individuals anticipate experiencing more positive than negative future events <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Newby-Clark & Ross, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: This tendency may reflect a broader optimism bias, whereby people systematically judge their future outcomes more favorably than their current circumstances (Weinstein, 1980; Sharot, 2011).
text.formatted: This tendency may reflect a broader optimism bias, whereby people systematically judge their future outcomes more favorably than their current circumstances <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Weinstein, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Sharot, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal evidence shows that individuals report higher expected well-being than current well-being, despite the relative stability of current well-being over time (Frijters et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Longitudinal evidence shows that individuals report higher expected well-being than current well-being, despite the relative stability of current well-being over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Frijters et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The magnitude and direction of expected well-being judgments vary with age.

Younger and middle-aged adults generally expect improvement in their well-being, whereas older adults tend to expect stability or decline across several well-being domains (Ryff, 1991; Lang et al., 2013; Hong et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Younger and middle-aged adults generally expect improvement in their well-being, whereas older adults tend to expect stability or decline across several well-being domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Ryff, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lang et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Hong et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Expectations about the future are linked to later health and well-being: anticipated positive personal events have been shown to explain variance in depression beyond current wellbeing (Edmondson et al., 2014) and, among adolescents, positive expectations of the future are associated with predicted healthier behaviors in young adulthood (McDade et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Expectations about the future are linked to later health and well-being: anticipated positive personal events have been shown to explain variance in depression beyond current wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Edmondson et al., 2014)</ref> and, among adolescents, positive expectations of the future are associated with predicted healthier behaviors in young adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(McDade et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Research on expected well-being specifically, however, has mostly examined it in relation to current well-being.
For example, this work has shown that, at the national level, the gap between expected and current well-being is larger in countries with less favorable societal functioning (Busseri, 2022).
text.formatted: For example, this work has shown that, at the national level, the gap between expected and current well-being is larger in countries with less favorable societal functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Busseri, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Less is known about which factors are associated with expected well-being itself, and whether they match those associated with current well-being.
This question matters for two reasons.

First, the meaning of the gap between current and expected well-being depends partly on what expected well-being reflects; if expected well-being draws on information that current well-being does not, the gap carries that information as well.

Second, expected wellbeing is often combined with current well-being in measures of population life evaluation wellbeing (e.g., Gallup, 2022), yet it is unclear what it contributes beyond current well-being.

As such, evidence on where the correlates of the two judgments converge or diverge would help clarify whether expected well-being largely restates current well-being or whether it captures aspects of people's lives that current well-being judgments miss.

To organize the broader range of variables that have been linked to well-being, we classified predictors into three conceptually distinct domains: past experiences, current circumstances, and identity and personality.
We included variables related to early life experiences or historical factors in the past experiences domain, including health growing up and childhood abuse.
We included variables related to present-day life conditions in the current circumstances domain, including age and physical health.
We included variables related to personality traits, psychological factors, and beliefs in the identity/personality domain, including extraversion and purpose in life.
Although variables within each of these domains are known to predict current well-being, the same cannot be said for expected well-being.
Past experiences provide individuals with autobiographical information that may serve as one information source for current and expected well-being.

Major historical events, like the COVID-19 pandemic, and childhood experiences, including childhood health, religious upbringing, parental relationships, adverse experiences, and living conditions, are associated with current subjective well-being in adulthood (Pitzer & Fingerman, 2010; Gassman-Pines et al., 2020; Bradshaw et al., 2007; Rohner & Veneziano, 2001; Amato, 1994; Wnuk 2021; Bamford et al. 2023; Rothwell & Davoodi, 2024; Chen & VanderWeele 2018; Gohm et al., 1998; Waters et al., 2008; Sobolewski & Amato, 2005).
text.formatted: Major historical events, like the COVID-19 pandemic, and childhood experiences, including childhood health, religious upbringing, parental relationships, adverse experiences, and living conditions, are associated with current subjective well-being in adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Pitzer & Fingerman, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Gassman-Pines et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bradshaw et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Rohner & Veneziano, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Amato, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wnuk 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bamford et al. 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Rothwell & Davoodi, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Chen & VanderWeele 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Gohm et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Waters et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Sobolewski & Amato, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Past positive events are associated with more positive expectations of one's future well-being, whereas past negative events are associated with more negative expectations (Sailer et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Past positive events are associated with more positive expectations of one's future well-being, whereas past negative events are associated with more negative expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Sailer et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wang et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals with better physical health, education, financial security, stronger social connections, stable employment, and community belonging generally report higher current wellbeing, whereas health problems and other life stressors are associated with lower current wellbeing (Haim-Litevsky, 2023; Diener & Chan, 2011; Hernandez et al., 2018; Bonanomi & Rosina, 2022; Minichino et al., 2013; Santini et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Individuals with better physical health, education, financial security, stronger social connections, stable employment, and community belonging generally report higher current wellbeing, whereas health problems and other life stressors are associated with lower current wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Haim-Litevsky, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Diener & Chan, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Hernandez et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bonanomi & Rosina, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Minichino et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Santini et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Demographic characteristics such as gender have also been linked to well-being, although these relationships are often more complex and may reflect broader social and contextual influences (Matud et al., 2019; Pinquart & Sörensen, 2001).
text.formatted: Demographic characteristics such as gender have also been linked to well-being, although these relationships are often more complex and may reflect broader social and contextual influences <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Matud et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Pinquart & Sörensen, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Whether these same circumstances contribute similarly to expected well-being judgments is less clear.

However, recent evidence suggests that income and education may play a particularly important role in expected well-being judgments because they increase individuals' perceived capacity to shape future outcomes (Mandel et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, recent evidence suggests that income and education may play a particularly important role in expected well-being judgments because they increase individuals' perceived capacity to shape future outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Mandel et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The identity and personality domain reflects relatively stable aspects of the individual, including demographic identities (e.g., gender, religious affiliation), personality traits, and enduring psychological dispositions.

These characteristics may shape how individuals interpret their lives. Schimmack et al. (2002) proposed that well-being judgments are in part based on chronically accessible sources of information; that is, information that is consistently retrieved when people evaluate their lives (e.g., reliance on relationship status and academic performance).
text.formatted: These characteristics may shape how individuals interpret their lives. <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Schimmack et al. (2002)</ref> proposed that well-being judgments are in part based on chronically accessible sources of information; that is, information that is consistently retrieved when people evaluate their lives (e.g., reliance on relationship status and academic performance).

text.text: Personality traits help determine which sources remain chronically accessible over time, thereby influencing which information is most readily retrieved and how that information is evaluated when forming well-being judgments (Schimmack et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Personality traits help determine which sources remain chronically accessible over time, thereby influencing which information is most readily retrieved and how that information is evaluated when forming well-being judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Schimmack et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, a person's identity and personality may shape how they interpret their life circumstances, which then influences their global evaluations of their life.
A broad range of stable characteristics are associated with current well-being.

Positive psychological characteristics, including positive affect, religiosity, and personality traits such as conscientiousness, openness to experience, and emotional stability, are positively associated with current well-being judgments (Sophie et al., 2022; Alkozei et al., 2018; Anglim et al., 2020; Villani et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Positive psychological characteristics, including positive affect, religiosity, and personality traits such as conscientiousness, openness to experience, and emotional stability, are positively associated with current well-being judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Sophie et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Alkozei et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Anglim et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Villani et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, anxiety, depression, and loneliness show negative associations (Seifert, 2024; Cao et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In contrast, anxiety, depression, and loneliness show negative associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Seifert, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Cao et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Because these characteristics influence how people interpret the present moment, they may also shape how individuals imagine and evaluate their future life.

For example, individuals with more positive conceptions of aging tend to expect their future wellbeing to exceed their current well-being, and these conceptions partially explain the association between age and the current-expected well-being gap (Busseri, 2024). In Choma et al.'s (2014) study, individuals who reported higher expected well-being relative to their current well-being reported less hope, which they attributed to wishful thinking.

text.text: Although one might alternatively organize these factors according to past, present, and future, future-oriented constructs such as optimism and hope are better conceptualized as relatively stable individual characteristics that influence how people interpret and project their lives into the future.
Accordingly, we include them within the identity and personality domain in this study.
Prior work has largely examined predictors of current or expected well-being within a single domain or in isolation.

This leaves open the question of how distinct predictor domains, including past experiences, current circumstances, and identity and personality, jointly and differentially relate to each type of judgment across diverse cultural contexts.

The present study used data from Wave 1 of the Global Flourishing Study (GFS; Johnson et al., 2024) to identify which well-being-related factors, organized across three domains (past circumstances, identity and personality, and current circumstances), most consistently predicted current versus expected well-being judgments.
text.formatted: The present study used data from Wave 1 of the Global Flourishing Study (GFS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Johnson et al., 2024)</ref> to identify which well-being-related factors, organized across three domains (past circumstances, identity and personality, and current circumstances), most consistently predicted current versus expected well-being judgments.

text.text: Given the large number of candidate predictors within each domain, our preregistered hypotheses (OSF registration DOI: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/VMTK9) were stated at the domain level.

text.text: First, we hypothesized that positive past experiences would be positively associated with both current and expected well-being.
Second, we hypothesized that positive aspects of identity and personality would be positively associated with current well-being.
Third, we hypothesized that positive current circumstances would be positively associated with current well-being.

We also preregistered two exploratory questions: whether past experiences would be associated with expected well-being when controlling for current well-being, and whether current circumstances would be associated with current well-being when controlling for expected well-being.
We extended these exploratory analyses to all three domains and both outcomes.

Together, these analyses identify where the correlates of current and expected well-being converge and diverge, as a step toward understanding the information people draw on when evaluating their present and future lives.
This study used data from Wave 1 of the Global Flourishing Study (GFS).

The GFS is a longitudinal study that examines factors contributing to human flourishing in a large, internationally diverse sample spanning 22 countries and territories, with approximately 200,000 participants enrolled at Wave 1 (Johnson et al., 2024; VanderWeele et al., 2025).

text.text: All eligible Wave 1 respondents in the finalized analysis dataset were included.
Analyses were conducted using complete cases for the variables entering each model.

The main analytic sample consisted of 98,412 participants (50,465 female [51.3%], 47,916 male [48.7%]; 31 participants did not report gender), with a mean age of 46.42 years (SD = 17.62, range = 18-99).
Our preregistration specified listwise deletion without imputation.

During analysis, we found that much of the missingness in several variables did not reflect genuine non-response: our cleaning script had coded substantive responses such as "Not relevant" and "Unsure" as missing, along with skips and true non-responses.
For six variables (CRITICAL, LIFE_APPROACH, GOD_PUNISH, TELL_BELIEFS, COMFORT_REL, LOVED_BY_GOD), these responses made up approximately 30-44% of the sample.
Combined with listwise deletion across the full 95-variable predictor set, this retained only 18% of respondents.
We addressed this by revising the variable set rather than introducing unpreregistered imputation.
Excluding the six variables increased the analytic sample to 98,412 respondents (48.5%).

Results were highly consistent across specifications: in the full SSVS models, every predictor selected under the preregistered specification was also selected under the revised specification except one (trait anxiousness, "anxious, easily upset," for current well-being); no predictor changed effect direction, and the same predictors met the magnitude threshold.
The revised specification selected additional predictors, all with small effects (|Avg Nonzero β| < .10).

text.text: A related issue affected nine variables on childhood and parental relationships (e.g., feeling loved by one's father growing up, mother's religious service attendance at age 12), where "does not apply" (plausibly reflecting the absence of a parental figure) was also coded as missing.
We retained these variables in both specifications, so respondents for whom they did not apply were excluded by listwise deletion.

We did not recode responses for two reasons: their missingness was substantially lower than for the six variables described above and representing them would require substantive decisions beyond the scope of this study.
We note this as a limitation.
Current well-being was assessed using the Life Evaluation: Today item from the Global Flourishing Study.
Participants were asked, "On which step of the ladder would you say you personally feel you stand at this time?"
Responses ranged from 0 (worst possible life) to 10 (best possible life), with higher scores indicating greater current well-being.
Expected well-being was assessed using the Life Evaluation: Five Years From Now item.
Participants were asked, "Just your best guess, on which step do you think you will stand in the future, say about five years from now?"
Responses ranged from 0 (worst possible life) to 10 (best possible life), with higher scores indicating greater expected well-being.
Predictor variables were organized into three preregistered domains: past experiences, current circumstances, and identity and personality (Table 1).

text.text: Of the 95 candidate predictors, 89 were retained in the primary analytic models reported in the main text (see Missing Data): 14 belonging to the past experiences domain, 43 to the current circumstances domain, and 32 to the identity/personality domain.
We did not include country-specific/conditional response variables.
Past experiences included variables that represent early life experiences or historical factors, such as adverse childhood experiences and health growing up.
Current circumstances included variables related to present-day life conditions, such as socioeconomic status and health.
Identity and personality included variables reflecting personal traits, psychological factors, and beliefs, such as belonging and extraversion.

text.text: For each predictor, we report three posterior summaries with 95% credible intervals.
The MIP indicates how reliably a predictor was selected.

The average beta is the mean coefficient across all posterior draws, including those in which the predictor was excluded, and serves as a shrinkage-adjusted estimate that combines selection uncertainty and effect size.
The average nonzero beta is the mean coefficient across only the draws in which the predictor was included and estimates effect size conditional on inclusion.

text.text: We entered all predictors simultaneously into models for two outcomes:, current and expected well-being.
Each outcome was modeled twice: unadjusted and residualized on the other well-being measure via ordinary least squares (OLS).
The residualized models test whether predictors retained evidence of association beyond the variance the two outcomes share.
Together, these made four full models.
We repeated this procedure within each preregistered predictor domain (past experiences, current circumstances, and identity and personality).
The resulting 12 domain-specific models test whether results held when predictors were evaluated within their own domain rather than against the full set.
No observations were excluded based on univariate or multivariate outlier flags, except for impossible values identified through the study codebook.
Primary analyses were unweighted because SSVS does not readily accommodate complex survey weights.

To quantify each preregistered domain's relative contribution, we nested linear models using the predictors selected (MIP >.50) in the full SSVS models, in which all predictors competed jointly for inclusion.

text.text: Given that the number of predictors selected differed across domains and no entry order could be justified a priori, we used leave-one-domain-out comparisons instead of a standard hierarchical regression.
For each outcome, we fit a full model containing all selected predictors and three reduced models, each omitting one domain.
Each domain's unique contribution was the difference in R² between the full and corresponding reduced model (ΔR²).
This approach credits each domain with the unique variance it explains and does not depend on an arbitrary entry order.
We report R², ΔR², and nested-model F-tests (F, df, p) for each domain and outcome; as an indicator of whether each ΔR² estimate differed significantly from zero, we report its associated F-tests

This tested whether domain contributions changed after accounting for the shared variance between current and expected well-being.
The preregistered analytic plan specified three variable selection approaches: grouppenalized regression, sparse group lasso, and Bayesian stochastic search variable selection (SSVS).
The original goal was to triangulate findings across complementary statistical frameworks and to identify predictions that showed consistent evidence across methods.
During implementation, however, we determined that the two penalized regression approaches were not sufficiently aligned with the study's primary inferential intent.
The study was designed to evaluate evidence for individual predictors of current and expected well-being and to compare predictor-specific patterns across outcomes.

However, the penalized group models were primarily optimized for prediction, and their selections were extremely sensitive to the broad groupings of predictors, correlations among conceptually similar variables, and the choice of regularization parameters.

Given the large sample size, non-zero coefficients did not provide useful evidence for specific predictor variables and, frankly, merely showed that variables in these domains were predictive of our outcomes.
We therefore report the SSVS analyses as the primary analytic approach.

SSVS more directly addresses the predictor-specific questions of our study by providing posterior inclusion probabilities for individual variables as well as posterior estimates of direction and uncertainty.
The preregistered predictor domains, outcome specifications, covariate adjustments, and posterior inclusion probability threshold of .5 were retained.
Because the final analyses provided here relied on a single modeling framework, we did not apply the preregistered criteria for convergence or robustness across methods.
Conclusions are instead based on the posterior evidence obtained from the SSVS models and should be interpreted as conditional on that framework.

The decision to omit the penalized models reflected closer evaluation of the alignment between the methods and the research question, rather than whether the omitted analyses supported the study hypotheses.
The development and revision of the analytic code, including the preregistered implementations of all three methods, are preserved in the project's timestamped GitHub commit history.
Additionally, results from the group penalized regression analysis and the group lasso are presented in the supplementary materials.

Twelve preregistered variables were excluded from the analyses because they were categorical or country-specific and could not be entered as single continuous predictors: country of residence, household income, employment status, political identification, region (three variables), religious affiliation (three variables), and self-identification (two variables).
Household income was recorded in country-specific categories; perceived difficulty living on present income and household expenses were included as indicators of financial circumstances.
In an exploratory analysis that was not preregistered, we examined whether the key associations reflected differences between countries.
We centered all variables within country and reestimated each full model using ordinary least squares regression, including the predictors selected in the corresponding SSVS model.

text.text: Our preregistered hypotheses were broad.
We expected favorable past experiences, favorable aspects of identity and personality, and favorable current circumstances to be associated with higher current and expected well-being.
We evaluated these hypotheses through the predictors selected in the SSVS models, and through each domain's unique contribution in the nested model comparisons.
Overall, the hypotheses were supported, although the strength of that support differed considerably across domains.

However, our cross-sectional design cannot test whether past experiences relate to well-being through current circumstances, so this interpretation remains tentative.
We found support for the identity/personality hypothesis.
The domain contributed unique variance to current well-being and expected well-being; predictors remained associated with each outcome after controlling for the other.
Happiness and life satisfaction were the strongest and most consistently selected predictors of both outcomes across the full and residualized models.
Additionally, hope for the future and expecting more good than bad were associated with expected well-being.
Personality traits were frequently selected but had small coefficients.
The predictors that exceeded the magnitude threshold share content with the outcome itself.

Happiness and life satisfaction are established indicators of subjective well-being (Diener et al., 1984; Oishi et al., 2021), and hope and optimism concern expectations about one's future, which is what expected well-being asks respondents to judge.

text.text: Their strong associations therefore partly reflect conceptual overlap with the outcome.
The hypothesis that favorable current circumstances would be associated with higher current well-being was also supported.

Greater difficulty living on present income was associated with lower current well-being, and other current circumstances variables, including physical health, education, and worthwhileness, were selected with smaller coefficients.
Our exploratory analyses showed that current circumstances were also associated with expected wellbeing.
After controlling for current well-being, the current circumstances domain contributed nearly twice as much unique variance to expected well-being as identity/personality did.

This suggests that expectations of more or less improvement in well-being than others with the same current well-being depend more on circumstances with clear implications for the future, such as age, health, and finances, than on past experiences and stable dispositions.
Altogether, the nested model comparisons suggest that the three domains are better understood as overlapping sources of well-being.
In both unadjusted models, most of the explained variance was shared across domains, and this pattern held when the analysis was restricted to predictors with MIP > .95.

text.text: People's past experiences, current circumstances, and identity/personality appear to be intertwined, and a large part of what predicts current and expected well-being cannot be attributed to any single domain.

The predictors most consistently exceeding the |β| > .10 threshold across models (happiness, life satisfaction, and, for expected well-being, hope for the future) are conceptually related evaluative constructs; their empirical overlap likely accounts for their consistent selection and comparatively large effect sizes.
text.formatted: The predictors most consistently exceeding the |β| > .10 threshold across models (happiness, life satisfaction, and, for expected well-being, hope for the future) are conceptually related evaluative constructs; their empirical overlap likely accounts for their consistent selection and comparatively large effect sizes.

text.text: Although a broad range of past, present, and identity-related factors showed reliable evidence of association with well-being, only a small subset, largely items that share content with the outcomes, show effects of a magnitude likely to be practically meaningful.
At the individual-predictor level, happiness and life satisfaction were associated with both outcomes in the unadjusted models and were the strongest correlates of current well-being.
Their associations with expected well-being fell below the magnitude threshold once current well-being was controlled for.
In other words, happiness and life satisfaction were associated with expected well-being mainly through their association with current well-being.
Age exhibited opposite associations with the two residualized outcomes in both the full and domain-specific models.

Among participants with the same current well-being, older participants reported lower expected well-being; among participants with the same expected well-being, older participants reported higher current well-being.
Thus, compared with younger participants, older participants' ratings of their expected well-being were closer to, or lower than, the ratings of their current well-being.

In the residualized domain-specific models, we found that, among participants with the same current well-being, those who reported greater hope for the future reported higher expected well-being; among participants with the same expected well-being, they reported lower current well-being.
That is, participants with greater hope for the future rated their expected well-being further above their current well-being.
This finding appears to diverge from the aforementioned findings of Choma et al. (2014), in which participants with lower hope perceived greater expected well-being than current well-being.
text.formatted: This finding appears to diverge from the aforementioned findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Choma et al. (2014)</ref>, in which participants with lower hope perceived greater expected well-being than current well-being.

text.text: However, our measures differ (life evaluation vs.
life satisfaction; hope for the future as a single item vs. hope as a full scale), and they used latent growth curve analyses instead.

Beyond life satisfaction and happiness, feelings about one's income, household income growing up, health growing up, and worthwhileness were the most consistently selected predictors for current well-being, though only in the domain-specific SSVS models.
For expected well-being, expecting good things in life, gratitude, physical health, and worthwhileness were the most consistently selected predictors, though only in the domainspecific SSVS models.
The distinct predictor profiles identified for each outcome provide empirical support for treating current and expected well-being as related but distinct judgments.

Expected well-being judgments carry independent associations with health, behavior, traits, and life outcomes beyond current well-being (Lang et al., 2013; Edmondson et al., 2014; McDade et al., 2011), and reflect a distinct forward-looking judgment process through which people construct imagined futures (Gilbert & Wilson, 2007).

text.text: Our findings regarding the relationship between age and current and expected well-being consistent with prior work, in that younger and middle-aged adults generally expect higher wellbeing in the future, whereas older adults tend to expected lower well-being (Ryff, 1991; Röcke & Lachman, 2008; Lang et al., 2013; Hong et al., 2019).

text.text: Our findings extend this work in two ways.
First, age remained among the strongest predictors of current and expected well-being when evaluated alongside 88 other predictors.
Second, the pattern held when differences between countries were removed, which indicates that it is not specific to a few national contexts.

Socioemotional selectivity theory proposes that as perceived time remaining in life narrows, motivational priorities shift from future-oriented expansion toward present-focused emotional regulation and meaning (Carstensen, 2006; Carstensen, 2021).
text.formatted: Socioemotional selectivity theory proposes that as perceived time remaining in life narrows, motivational priorities shift from future-oriented expansion toward present-focused emotional regulation and meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Carstensen, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Carstensen, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: A shrinking time horizon may similarly recalibrate what a well-being judgment represents for an older versus a younger respondent.
Additionally, prior research demonstrates that people's conceptions of aging partially account for the relationship between age and expected well-being (Busseri, 2024).
text.formatted: Additionally, prior research demonstrates that people's conceptions of aging partially account for the relationship between age and expected well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Busseri, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, we posit that age's association with well-being judgments may in part reflect normative beliefs about aging and shifts in motivational orientation.
Current and expected well-being judgments may share a common evaluative process instead of reflecting fundamentally distinct cognitive operations.

However, the divergence in specific predictors and their magnitude across outcomes suggests that the specific sources of information weighted within that process may differ depending on the temporal dimension of life evaluation (ie., now versus in five years).
Experimental and process-level research would be needed to directly test this interpretation.
These interpretations are constrained by several methodological limitations.
First, the cross-sectional design reflects associations at a single time point and cannot establish whether identified predictors causally influence well-being judgments.

Second, analyses were conducted on complete cases (N = 98,412 of 202, 897 surveyed); missing data patterns may limit the representativeness of findings within the broader GFS sample (see Missing Data).

Relatedly, several country-or religion-specific items were excluded from analyses due to their conditional administration, which may limit the study's ability to capture culturally or religion-specific predictors of well-being.

Third, primary analyses were conducted without sampling weights, since the regularization-based methods used here do not accommodate complex survey design features; this may limit generalizability at the population level.
Fourth, both outcomes and most predictors rely on self-report, and shared method variance may inflate observed associations.

Fifth, while SSVS reliably identifies predictors that consistently appear across posterior samples, it identifies associations rather than mechanisms; the present study cannot speak to the cognitive or psychological process through which identified predictors influence well-being judgments.
Finally, our analyses pooled respondents from 22 countries, and the variable selection did not account for country of residence.

Although the key associations were similar in within-country OLS models, those models used the predictors selected from the pooled sample, so we cannot rule out that selection itself would differ within countries.
Future country-specific analyses will help clarify how consistent these patterns are across cultural contexts.

Despite these limitations, the present study demonstrates the utility of data-driven variable selection approaches for identifying reliable predictors of well-being outcomes across large, high-dimensional datasets.
This approach may complement traditional theory-driven hypothesis testing in well-being research.

text.text: Support for the past experiences hypothesis was the weakest.
Several past experiences variables were selected in the SSVS models, and the domain contributed unique variance in every nested model.
However, no past experiences variable met the magnitude threshold in the full model, and the domain's unique contribution to the nested models was small.
Only health growing up met the threshold, and only when predictors were evaluated within their own domain.
Therefore, we regard this hypothesis as weakly supported.
This pattern does not imply that childhood is unimportant for well-being.

text.text: Several directions for future research follow from the present findings.

Longitudinal follow-up using subsequent GFS waves would allow direct tests of whether today's predictors of expected well-being actually forecast later reported well-being, and whether people's expectations become more accurate over time.

Cross-lagged panel models would allow further examination of bidirectional relationships between current and expected well-being across time.Future work should also examine country-level variation in predictor profiles; the GFS offers a unique opportunity to identify culture-specific predictors of each judgment.
Experimental and experience sampling approaches would help clarify the cognitive and affective processes underlying current and expected judgments more directly.

Future work incorporating direct measures of future time perspective, goals, values, and motivations may better characterize why age relates to these judgments as it does.ConclusionExpected well-being judgments have received comparatively less attention than current well-being in the literature.

The present findings suggest that these judgments warrant greater attention, as the factors associated with how people evaluate their lives today may not fully explain how they anticipate their lives unfolding in the future.
Although current and expected well-being judgments shared many correlates, several factors showed different patterns of association across the two outcomes.
Current and expected well-being judgments draw on overlapping sources of information, but those sources may be weighted differently depending on the temporal dimension of the judgment.
These findings raise important questions regarding the mechanisms of these judgments.
For example, how do perceptions of household income shape expected well-being judgments and through what pathways?
What is the link between age, physical health, and expected well-being judgments, beyond their associations with current wellbeing?
